title: #WhatIEatinaDay: The Quality, Accuracy, and Engagement of Nutrition Content on TikTok
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 250 randomly sampled nutrition TikTok posts in which each post's accuracy was scored against external evidence-based nutrition guidelines (Australian Dietary Guidelines, Nutrient Reference Values, Practice-based Evidence in Nutrition) on a five-level scale. Table 1 gives verbatim counts: 47 of 197 assessable posts (24%) completely inaccurate and 45 (23%) mostly inaccurate. Items judged against an external ground truth and reported as a share = CONTENT. The parallel Social Media Evaluation Checklist results are QUALITY and are not extracted.

estimates.country: not stated; TikTok content was not geographically restricted, and accuracy was judged against Australian dietary guidance
estimates.date: posts published September 2023 to March 2024; collected April 2024
estimates.measure_type: % of assessable nutrition TikTok posts rated completely inaccurate against evidence-based nutrition guidelines
estimates.denominator: 197 of the 250 sampled posts that were assessable for accuracy (53 presented nutrition content with no information, advice or commentary and were scored not assessable); the 250 were randomly drawn from 1,054 eligible posts found through nutrition hashtag searches
estimates.definition: Post scored 'completely inaccurate' on the Denniss and Lindberg accuracy protocol when checked against the Australian Dietary Guidelines, Nutrient Reference Values and Practice-based Evidence in Nutrition
estimates.misinfo_def: "the accuracy of the information presented was scored as 'completely inaccurate', 'mostly inaccurate, some accuracies', 'mostly accurate, some inaccuracies', 'completely accurate' and 'not assessable'"
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Three researchers independently reviewed posts against the defined criteria and discussed discrepancies to reach consensus; accuracy was graded against national dietary guidelines and evidence grades A-D per NHMRC criteria. No kappa or other agreement statistic is reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: The accuracy of nutrition-related information in social media posts was evaluated using the research protocol developed by Denniss, Lindberg [25]. This involved evaluating content against evidence-based nutrition guidelines, including the Australian Dietary Nutrients 2025, 17, 781 5 of 13 Guidelines, Nutrient Reference Values, and Practice-based Evidence in Nutrition.
estimates.notes: Kept the Table 1 value because it is backed by verbatim counts (47 of 197) rather than a rounded percentage. denom_selection=curated because the eligible pool came from in-app hashtag searches and the authors state the algorithm 'may have led to an overrepresentation of highly engaged, viral, or controversial posts'; the draw of 250 from 1,054 was itself random. Confidence is medium, not high, because the paper's own accuracy numbers disagree across Abstract, Results and Table (see missed_or_uncertain).

missed_or_uncertain: IMPORTANT INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY. The paper reports its headline accuracy result three times with three different sets of numbers. Abstract: 'A total of 36% of posts were considered completely accurate, while 24% were mostly inaccurate, and 18% completely inaccurate.' Results section 3.2: 14% completely accurate, 29% mostly accurate, 18% mostly inaccurate, 19% completely inaccurate, 20% not assessable (sums to 100% of 250). Table 1: of 197 assessable posts, completely accurate 33 (17%), mostly accurate 72 (37%), mostly inaccurate 45 (23%), completely inaccurate 47 (24%). The Abstract's 36% completely accurate is irreconcilable with both other sources and appears to be the mostly-accurate share of assessable posts mislabelled; its 24% and 18% look like the completely-inaccurate share of assessable posts and the mostly-inaccurate share of all 250, again mislabelled. I anchored the extraction on Table 1, the only place with counts. A second contradiction: Results say 'No statistical significance was observed in engagement metrics across different levels of accuracy or evidence (p > 0.05)', while the Discussion says 'completely inaccurate posts garnered significantly higher likes, comments, shares, and saves than accurate posts (p < 0.05)'. A third: weight-loss posts are 29% completely inaccurate in Results and 28% in the Discussion. Not extracted, with reasons: (1) Social Media Evaluation Checklist results (82% lacked transparent advertising, 77% did not disclose conflicts of interest, 63% promoted stereotypical attitudes, 55% did not provide evidence-based information, 75% lacked balanced accurate content, 90% did not point out risks and benefits, 48% used testimonials, 98% accurately reflected their message) are QUALITY under section 3 - none judges a claim true or false against a ground truth, and the denominator is 'applicable posts', which is never given as a number. (2) Evidence grades A-D (12% Grade A, 12% Grade B, 20% Grade C, 15% Grade D, 41% not assessable) grade the strength of supporting evidence, not the truth of the claim, so also QUALITY. (3) Accuracy breakdowns by nutrition topic (weight loss 18% mostly inaccurate and 29% completely inaccurate; food/nutrient/supplement 33% mostly inaccurate; goal-oriented 29%; general nutrition 29% completely accurate and 43% mostly accurate; recipes 50% not assessable) and by creator type (content farms 18% mostly inaccurate and 30% completely inaccurate; health and wellness creators 25% completely inaccurate; fitness creators 23% and 18%; dietitians 42% completely accurate) are subgroup splits read off Figures 3 and 4 with denominators that are never stated, so I left them out; they are the paper's secondary analyses, not its headline. (4) Creator-type and topic composition shares (health and wellness influencers 32%, fitness 18%, dietitians 5%, weight loss 34%, recipes 31-32%) describe who posts and about what, not prevalence of misinformation. (5) Engagement means by accuracy level are scale means with no share attached. (6) Country cannot be assigned: the sample is not geographically restricted, though the accuracy standard is Australian. NOTE ON QUOTES: in this text file most body lines appear twice and running heads are spliced into sentences, so no sentence longer than one printed line survives as a contiguous span. Quotes are exact whitespace-collapsed spans of the file, which is why row 0's moderator_quote contains the running head "Nutrients 2025, 17, 781 5 of 13" mid-sentence and row 1's quote starts mid-sentence. Table 1's accuracy block is quoted in full (engagement columns included) because the counts and their percentages sit on the same contiguous run.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of TikTok. Nutrition hashtag searches (#healthyeating, #healthyfood, #diet, #weightlosstips and others, piloted and refined) were run in April 2024 from newly created accounts in a private browser to limit personalisation, covering posts published September 2023 - March 2024; PRISMA-ScR-style screening produced 1,054 eligible posts, from which 250 were randomly selected in Excel. Posts were categorised by nutrition topic and creator type by three researchers independently with discrepancies resolved by consensus (no reliability coefficient reported). Accuracy was scored on the five-level Denniss and Lindberg protocol against the Australian Dietary Guidelines, Nutrient Reference Values and Practice-based Evidence in Nutrition; evidence strength was graded A-D on NHMRC criteria; quality was scored on a modified Social Media Evaluation Checklist. 53 of 250 posts (20%) were not assessable for accuracy and 41% were not assessable for evidence. Authors' stated limitations: public posts only, keyword reliance may miss algospeak, and TikTok's recommendation algorithm probably over-represented highly engaged, viral or controversial posts. The paper's numbers are internally inconsistent across Abstract, Results and Table 1, and the Discussion contradicts the Results on the engagement significance test.
rob.item6_quote: As per the protocol, the accuracy of the information presented was scored as "completely inaccurate", "mostly inaccurate, some accuracies", "mostly accurate, some inaccuracies", "completely accurate" and "not assessable" (Supplementary Table S4) [25].
